tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper compares KVell against RocksDB 6.2 (plus PebblesDB, TokuMX, WiredTiger) on YCSB and Nutanix workloads. Not A: the repo has only KVell-side YCSB code and scripts (workload-ycsb.c, scripts/run-aws.sh), with no RocksDB or competitor harness; the paper names no CPU models ('2.4GHz Intel Xeon', '4.2GHz Intel i7') and gives no compiler or flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: throughput at least 2x the closest competitor (RocksDB 6.2, PebblesDB, TokuMX, WiredTiger) on read-dominated workloads and 5x on write-dominated workloads; on mostly-scan workloads comparable or better; maximum latencies an order of magnitude lower than the best competitor, even on scan-based workloads. Body (Config-Optane, 100M 1KB items): YCSB A 8x RocksDB and 5.8x PebblesDB (next best); YCSB B/C 2.2x/2.7x over existing KVs; Nutanix production workloads ~4x RocksDB (the next best); uniform YCSB E roughly equal to RocksDB (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper states none. Repo Makefile defaults: clang with CFLAGS=-O2 -ggdb3 -Wall (clang++ -std=c++11 for index code); README recommends TCMalloc (gperftools). Not confirmed as the build used for the paper runs.
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper. The paper states no compiler or flags, and the repo Makefile defaults to clang -O2. CPU models are not named. The repo reproduces only the KVell side (scripts/run-aws.sh, sample_results); the RocksDB/PebblesDB/TokuMX/WiredTiger runs have no published harness. Scans are weaker: RocksDB wins with small items, and uniform YCSB E is about equal (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s). The latest commit (2025-12-15) only fixes random-number generation in a workload generator; before that the last commit was 2020-11, and the 'osdi' branch holds KVell+ (OSDI'20).

notes: The claim matches the paper abstract. I made the latency wording precise ('maximum', not 'tail') and added per-workload RocksDB numbers from the body. The metadata checked out: MIT, 293 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-12-15 (active). I opened the benchmark PDF through raw.githubusercontent (same file as the blob URL).

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed USENIX ATC'20 paper measures MatrixKV against RocksDB (RocksDB-SSD and RocksDB-L0-NVM) with db_bench and YCSB. The repo ships db_bench scripts (test_sh/). Not A: the CPU is only 'two Genuine Intel(R) 2.20GHz 24-core processors' with no model, and no compiler or flags are stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: 3.6x higher random-write throughput and 5x lower 99th-percentile latency than RocksDB (2.6x / 1.9x vs NoveLSM). Paper body: random-write throughput (db_bench, 80GB, 4KB values) is 3.6x RocksDB-L0-NVM (RocksDB with an 8GB L0 in NVM; 1.86x-3.61x across 64B-64KB values) and 2.6x NoveLSM; YCSB load 3.29x RocksDB-L0-NVM. YCSB-A p99 latency (Table 2: 405us vs 786/2080/11055us) is 1.9x lower than RocksDB-L0-NVM, 5x lower than NoveLSM, and 27x lower than stock RocksDB-SSD, so the abstract's latency pairing is swapped relative to the body.
corrections.hardware: Two Intel 2.20GHz 24-core processors (model not named), 32GB DRAM, 800GB Intel SSDSC2BB800G7 SSD, 2x128GB Intel Optane DC PMM (8GB NVM used per store); Fedora 27, Linux 4.13.9
corrections.workload: db_bench micro-benchmarks: 80GB of KV pairs (16B keys, 4KB default values, 64B-64KB sweep) inserted in uniform random order, then sequential writes and random/sequential reads; YCSB load plus workloads A-F (80GB load, 1M ops each); tail latency from YCSB-A at ~20K req/s. Each hybrid store limited to 8GB NVM, with RocksDB defaults (64MB memtable, 256MB L1, AF 10).
corrections.caveats: Code is a diff against RocksDB v5.18.3 (the README gives the RocksDB commit to reset against); it is not a GitHub fork. The main RocksDB baseline in the paper is RocksDB-L0-NVM, i.e. RocksDB given the same 8GB NVM for L0; stock RocksDB-SSD is slower still. The abstract's 5x/1.9x p99 figures are paired with the wrong baselines relative to Table 2. Reads and sequential writes are roughly equal to RocksDB, not faster. No compiler, flags or CPU model given. Needs Optane DC PMM and PMDK. License: GitHub detects GPL-2.0, but the repo keeps RocksDB's COPYING (GPLv2) and LICENSE.Apache, and RocksDB-derived files carry dual GPLv2/Apache-2.0 headers; MatrixKV-added files (e.g. include/rocksdb/nvm_option.h) have no header. Unmaintained since 2020.

notes: The record faithfully reflects the USENIX abstract, but the body shows 3.6x is against RocksDB-L0-NVM and the p99 multipliers are swapped (1.9x vs RocksDB-L0-NVM, 27x vs stock RocksDB). I corrected the claim and pointed benchmark_url at the full paper PDF. Metadata verified: 76 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit on every branch 2020-08-07 (abandoned). License corrected to RocksDB's dual license.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'17 paper reports PebblesDB at 6.7x RocksDB's write throughput on db_bench, and the db_bench code ships in the repo. Not A: the paper gives the CPU only as 'Intel Xeon 2.8 GHz' with no model and states no compiler or flags; the README's g++ versions are a build requirement, not the benchmark build.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SOSP'17 paper: on db_bench micro-benchmarks PebblesDB gets 6.7x RocksDB's write throughput (single-threaded random writes, 50M keys, 1KB values) and 27% higher read throughput, with 2.4-3x less write IO. With 4 writer threads it gets 3.3x RocksDB's write throughput (RocksDB default config). Inserting 50M values: 56.18 vs 14.12 KOps/s (~4.0x, derived from page data). README rounds this to '6x the write throughput of RocksDB ... 50% lesser IO'. Sequential writes are ~3x slower and seek-only range queries ~30% slower than HyperLevelDB on a fully compacted store.
corrections.hardware: Dell Precision Tower 7810, Intel Xeon 2.8 GHz (model not named), 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04 / Linux 4.4, ext4 on software RAID0 over two Intel 750 1.2TB SSDs
corrections.caveats: benchmark.md shows only relative-throughput graphs (normalized to HyperLevelDB) with no '6x' text. The 6x/50%-IO line is in the README, and exact numbers and hardware are in the SOSP'17 paper. CPU model not named; compiler and flags for the benchmark runs not stated. Weaker on sequential inserts (~3x slower) and on seek-heavy range queries on a compacted store. Derived from HyperLevelDB, but not a GitHub fork. The last commit on every branch is 2019-08-03 (the 2024-04-16 date was a pushed_at timestamp, not a commit).

notes: benchmark.md compares against RocksDB only in graphs; its Random-Writes bars (~2.75 vs ~0.41 relative to HyperLevelDB) agree with the paper's 6.7x. I repointed benchmark_url to the paper, which states the numbers. I corrected last_commit (2024-04-16 was pushed_at; the real last commit is 2019-08-03) and maintenance to abandoned. BSD-3-Clause and 521 stars check out. I left is_fork_of as HyperLevelDB, because the README says PebblesDB was built by modifying it.
